title: A Case of Cognitive Decline Resulting from Aging, Temporal Lobe Epilepsy, and Environmental Factors
case_prompt:
A 63-year-old Caucasian woman was admitted for ambulatory electroencephalography to assess her temporal lobe epilepsy. She has had focal seizures since age 10, characterized by déjà vu, dissociation, olfactory hallucinations (“smelling metal”), and prodromal nausea, sweating, palpitations, blank stares, greying of vision and a one-minute postictal confusion. She denied lip-smacking or incontinence. She was treated with valproic acid until recently switched to levetiracetam.

Over the past few years, she developed progressive memory problems: missing appointments, forgetting names and conversations, getting lost in familiar surroundings, and misplacing household items. She reports significant anxiety and low self-esteem due to these lapses. She sometimes recalls events with cueing but remains uncertain. She has no other medical history, occasional alcohol use, no tobacco or recreational drugs, and a family history notable only for essential tremor in maternal relatives.

On examination, she was alert, oriented to person and place but disoriented to time. She appeared slightly anxious without abnormal movements. Speech, mood, and affect were normal; thought processes were circumstantial with mild disorganization. No psychosis or suicidal ideation. She was insightful and cooperative.

A baseline Montreal Cognitive Assessment score was 25/30, losing five points on delayed recall and showing visuospatial difficulties remediable with cueing; prior MoCA scores had declined from 29/30 in 2013 to 25/30 in 2017. 

Investigations included a 3-day ambulatory EEG showing mild bitemporal slowing without electrographic seizures; routine blood tests (CBC, LFTs, TSH, electrolytes, B12, BUN, creatinine) were normal. Brain MRI showed minimal microvascular ischemic changes without infarction or hemorrhage. 

Neuropsychological testing (WAIS-IV) revealed intact verbal reasoning (87th percentile) but impaired visuospatial skills (27th percentile) and processing speed (6th percentile). She exhibited below-average performance on new visuospatial tasks and the lowest scores on delayed recall (verbal and visual) and recognition testing, consistent with a neurologic memory impairment.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Delirium considered — “presence of acute memory impairment along with … executive functioning impairment with attention deficit and fluctuation of the symptoms indicates delirium as the most likely diagnosis.”  
2. Dementia/Alzheimer’s disease considered — “if memory impairment presents without an acute onset, attention deficit, or fluctuations, then dementia is the most likely diagnosis.”  
3. Mild cognitive impairment favored over AD — “Compared to the controls, all measures of memory … were significantly impaired in individuals with MCI; … there was no significant difference in general cognition (measured by the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale-Revised) between patients with MCI and the controls.”  
4. Metabolic and nutritional causes excluded — “Before diagnosing a patient with MCI, it is important to rule out … hyponatremia and hypercalcemia; thyroid disorders; cobalamin deficiency; and alcohol dependence, which have been associated with cognitive impairment.”  
5. Temporal lobe epilepsy–related memory loss considered — “TLE cannot be ruled out from being an etiology for her cognitive impairment, irrespective of the fact that the ambulatory EEG did not reveal significant findings.”
